title: The AI Engineering Skills Map for Knowledge Workers
dek: Cursor takes on GitHub with Origin, Anthropic's leaked $65 billion run rate sets up the IPO valuation fight, and Stripe closes its $7 billion OpenRouter deal — then the main event: NLW's five-skill AI engineering map for knowledge workers, from capability mapping to rapid skill acquisition, all resting on a foundation of domain judgment.

oneIdea.headline: We're moving from doing our work to managing agents that do our work — and that shift demands five new skills.
oneIdea.summary: AI capability mapping. Context and harness management. Problem and product prototyping. New opportunity identification. Rapid new skill acquisition. Inspired by Andrew Ng's AI engineering skills map for developers, this is the knowledge-worker version — and it only works layered on a foundation of domain judgment, whether personal, borrowed from colleagues, or embedded in rubrics and context. None of it can simply be handed to you; you learn it by doing.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: Capability mapping is a clinical governance skill, and nobody can hand it to you
items.body: The first of the five skills — knowing what the tool is natively good at, and where Mollick's jagged frontier runs — describes something every GP using a scribe has already been doing informally. The scribe is excellent on a single-problem consultation and quietly poor on the ten-minute appointment that turns out to contain four problems, a safeguarding hint and a medication reconciliation. NLW's point is that you only learn where the edge is by trial and error, because your particular caseload may break the received wisdom. That is worth saying out loud in a practice meeting, because at the moment this mapping lives in individual heads. Writing down, even crudely, which consultation types we check line by line and which we skim is cheap, and it is the sort of thing a CQC inspector will eventually ask to see.

items.title: Skill three in a surgery is not software engineering — it is the recall list you never got round to
items.body: "Building the thing that does the work" sounds absurd in general practice until you translate it. It is not writing an EMIS module; it is producing the search, the audit, the recall cohort or the small dashboard that currently waits months for somebody with the time. If NLW is right that this is the biggest shift knowledge work has seen, the practical consequence for a practice is that clinical staff can specify and iterate their own queries rather than joining a queue, with the CCG or supplier reviewing rather than building. If Zitron is right that the whole thing is running on subsidised compute, the same capability is real but rented, and anything we build should be exportable and re-creatable by hand. Either way the constraint is not the tool. It is information governance and who signs off a query that touches identifiable data.

items.title: The apprenticeship problem is our problem, and it arrives sooner in training practices
items.body: NLW closes on the question of how the next generation develops domain judgment if experienced workers use AI to do what juniors previously did. In GP training that is not hypothetical. Deciding what mattered in a consultation and committing it to the record is how a registrar learns to think, and a scribe that drafts a competent note removes exactly that friction. His tentative answer — treat AI as multiplayer, with the small team rather than the individual as the unit — maps neatly onto how we already teach: joint surgeries, tutorials on the notes, random case analysis. The cheap adjustment is to have registrars write the problem list and the plan themselves before the draft is accepted, and to use the difference between the two as the teaching material. That is worth doing whichever way the economics fall.

the_other_side.text: Zitron never engages the skills thesis on its own terms — his piece is a capital-markets argument about whether OpenAI can meet its obligations — but it lands directly underneath it. His claim is that the token-hungry way of working this episode describes is currently being paid for by the vendors rather than the users: the labs sell inference far below cost, and the revenue exists only by "allowing users to burn $14,000 a month in tokens for $200". He points to enterprises moved onto accounts "that required them to pay the actual cost" and then stalling, and to Ramp data showing customers "slow to adopt Anthropic's more-expensive 'Fable' model because of the price". The conclusion is that this demand is shallow and price-elastic — "customers are becoming cost-conscious at exactly the time they need to be spending more" — so the working habits being formed now may not survive being priced properly.

the_truth_beneath.text: The single variable both men orbit is the unit cost of running an agent set against the value of the work it displaces. Both accept as fact that inference is currently sold below cost and that usage is climbing very fast. The empirical question that will resolve is what happens when an ordinary knowledge worker's agent habit is priced at cost, and the observable that settles it is renewal behaviour on unsubsidised, metered enterprise contracts — whether seats and token budgets grow once the discounts expire. The residue is pure worldview: Whittemore assumes capability compounds faster than price; Zitron assumes the price is the product. Whittemore is vindicated if unsubsidised agent use keeps growing and something like his five skills turns up in real hiring specs; Zitron if metered accounts flatten and token-maxxing budgets quietly lapse. Both are polemicists with incentives — Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — and the signal is where they agree despite opposite priors: today's token prices are not the real ones. Watch enterprise renewals after the discounts end.

headlines.headline: Cursor takes on GitHub with Origin
headlines.summary: Cursor's new repo hosting platform is Git hosting plus better integrations for the coding agents you're already using — natural language queries across the code base, agents handling comments and commits, all without context switching or connectors. The launch is an early preview for existing customers.

headlines.headline: As if on cue, GitHub went down for six hours
headlines.summary: Maybe Origin's biggest pitch is platform stability — GitHub's service has been widely perceived to be degrading over the past year, and right around the announcement it suffered a six-hour degradation. SpaceX AI's Matt Palmer quipped they'd have shipped earlier 'but GitHub was down.' At this point, complaining about GitHub is basically part of being a developer.

headlines.headline: You can now host your repos in Cursor Origin and deploy to Vercel — and unlike GitHub, it's online.
headlines.summary: The Vercel CEO piling on GitHub's outage in the middle of Origin's launch window — a rival platform boss twisting the knife on the incumbent's weakest point.

headlines.headline: Origin's answer to lock-in: don't switch, mirror
headlines.summary: Cursor knows moving code is extremely hard, so Origin supports mirroring — leave your code on GitHub, let Origin sync it, and detach later if you like it. GitHub stays the system of record, theoretically minimizing the risk of breaking production workflows. Skeptics still want a longer security and infra track record before moving customer projects over.

headlines.headline: There's real demand for an agent-first GitHub — but the bar is brutally high
headlines.summary: A GitHub built from the ground up assuming agents push most of the code is what has people interested: triggering agents on code changes, running scheduled tasks from a single platform. If nothing else, the response shows the demand is there — but that doesn't make Origin's path easier, because ripping out core infrastructure like GitHub asks a huge amount of users.

headlines.headline: Cursor is shipping straight through the SpaceX acquisition
headlines.summary: Acquisitions stereotypically slow the acquired company's innovation; SpaceX AI seems determined for that not to be the case, with Origin landing just as the deal closes and Grok 4.6 billed as an early look at what the two will build together. The division of labor, per Cursor's blog: 'SpaceX is building the computing capacity needed to scale intelligence far beyond what exists today. Cursor will be one place where that intelligence becomes useful.'

headlines.headline: Anthropic's leaked run rate: $65 billion
headlines.summary: Sources who've seen the investor update say Anthropic hit a $65 billion revenue run rate at the end of July — a sevenfold increase since the beginning of the year and roughly a 40% jump since the $47 billion figure disclosed in May.

headlines.headline: 550% growth — and some investors are bummed
headlines.summary: The numbers matter because of the astronomical IPO valuation Anthropic is seeking: some investors expect $2 trillion, with some quoting an 800% growth rate to justify even more. The new figures put annualized growth at 550% — incredibly strong but slowing versus the first half — prompting author Tae Kim to remind everyone you can't extrapolate month-over-month growth acceleration to infinity. 'This is still insane growth.'

headlines.headline: OpenAI plus Anthropic: $100 billion in run rate
headlines.summary: Combine Anthropic's $65 billion with the $40 billion annualized run rate OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar has been reporting and the two companies are at roughly $100 billion in revenue run rate — up from low single-digit billions at this time last year.

headlines.headline: Stripe's OpenRouter deal is official: $7 billion
headlines.summary: Below the rumored $10 billion, but a huge markup for OpenRouter, which last raised at $1.3 billion in May. The immediate discourse: did Stripe overpay for an AI gateway it could arguably build itself?

headlines.headline: The $7B test: does it move Stripe's own valuation 5%?
headlines.summary: Against the 'surely Stripe can build its own gateway' chorus, one fintech engineer argued the crowd is anchoring on the wrong number: big acquirers pay relative to their own market cap, not the target's standalone worth — see Facebook/WhatsApp or SpaceX/Cursor. If buying OpenRouter improves Stripe's valuation prospects by more than five percent, the price pays for itself; competitive tension is how five billion becomes seven.

headlines.headline: Everyone is overthinking this: tokens are the new currency, and Stripe is the plumbing
headlines.summary: Stripe views itself as the core financial plumbing of the internet economy, and tokens are a new essential currency in that economy. Not all tokens are equal, users need to move easily between categories of them, and OpenRouter is the leading company doing that. To get the customers, infrastructure, and brand online immediately, you pay the price it takes to get the deal done — and my guess is it pays off for Stripe in big ways.

headlines.headline: The AI engineering skills map for knowledge workers
headlines.summary: Knowledge work is moving from doing our work to managing agents that do our work. The five skills that matter in that transition: AI capability mapping, context and harness management, problem and product prototyping, new opportunity identification, and rapid new skill acquisition. Combined with a foundation of domain judgment, you get a knowledge worker more capable and more powerful than ever before.

headlines.headline: The inspiration: Andrew Ng's map for developers
headlines.summary: Ng's four AI engineering skills — building and deploying AI applications, software engineering fundamentals, using coding agents, and shaping the build — are his answer to a noisy, hype-filled information environment. The key insight: even if agents write the code, deeply understanding software (cost, scalability, reliability, speed trade-offs) still drives better stack, architecture, and testing decisions. Foundations still matter; agentic coding is now its own skill on top.

headlines.headline: Domain judgment doesn't leave when AI arrives
headlines.summary: The foundation under all five skills is the ability to define quality, recognize trade-offs, understand consequences, and take responsibility for decisions. Just because ChatGPT can write the copy and make the ad assets doesn't mean someone with no marketing experience can plan and execute a campaign well — and it's not marketing in general that matters, it's marketing in the context of your organization, the stuff that never got encoded into training data.

headlines.headline: Judgment comes in three flavors: personal, borrowed, and embedded
headlines.summary: Domain judgment doesn't exclusively come from 10 or 20 years in a field. There's personal judgment — standards and pattern recognition you've internalized; borrowed judgment — expertise supplied through collaboration, review, and shared decision-making; and embedded judgment — expertise captured in examples, rubrics, policies, and evaluations you feed the AI.

headlines.headline: Skill one: mapping the jagged frontier
headlines.summary: AI can blow you away one minute and make a mistake the next that you wouldn't expect from the least capable intern — Ethan Mollick's 'jagged frontier.' Capability mapping means knowing what AI is natively good at, when a task needs an assisted approach versus workflow automation versus a truly agentic solution, which models and effort levels suffice, and how much human oversight is needed. Nobody can hand it to you; you learn it by trial and error, because your particular tasks may break the conventional wisdom.

headlines.headline: Skill two: set the AI up for success
headlines.summary: Context management is making sure the AI has the information it needs — past campaign performance, analytics, customer feedback — rather than a bare prompt and a prayer. The harness is everything else surrounding the model: instructions, documents, tool access, permissions, memory. Some of this is governed by your organization, but a lot is customized per worker — and today's best practices will almost inevitably have changed six months from now.

headlines.headline: Skill three: build the thing that does the work
headlines.summary: Not marketers becoming software engineers — but when everyone can push code, a lot of previous work gets done differently. Instead of manually pulling campaign data from every platform into Excel, a marketer can build an internal dashboard plus the engine underneath it, ingesting via APIs with AI surfacing the first layer of insights. Domain judgment still supplies the translation layer to real actionable insight — but a huge amount of time is freed up for exactly that judgment-style work.

headlines.headline: Building things instead of doing things may be the biggest shift knowledge work has ever seen
headlines.summary: Knowledge workers should not think of themselves as turning into full product managers and software engineers — but being able to build things to solve problems and do parts of our jobs is perhaps the most significant shift in how knowledge work happens that we've ever experienced. If you've been on the fence, go messily clunk your way through Codex and Claude Code and figure out which parts of your work could be transformed.

headlines.headline: Skill four: agents bring forward the infinite backlog
headlines.summary: If skill three is using code to solve existing problems, skill four asks what's newly possible: every knowledge worker has an endless list of things they'd do if time and resources were no limit, and agents make a much bigger portion of it viable. One useful trick: imagine your organization handed you a team of software engineers to do whatever you want with. Before long you hit totally net-new ideas — think small-company marketing teams building and releasing games as top of funnel.

headlines.headline: Skill five: learning itself becomes continuous
headlines.summary: The meta-skill that cuts across the rest: recognizing which adjacent skills have suddenly become valuable, creating space to experiment and learn by doing in real-world environments, and assessing whether the output is worth integrating into how you work. Skill acquisition becomes not the work of semi-regular upskilling seminars but a continuous, ongoing process — and there's far less inertia in how you work than in how your organization does.

headlines.headline: The apprenticeship problem — and a multiplayer answer
headlines.summary: If experienced workers use AI to do what younger workers previously did, how does the next generation ever develop domain judgment? One answer worth exploring: shift from thinking about AI as single-player to AI as multiplayer, with the core unit of AI moving outside the individual to the small team. A subject for a future show.
